font.b: In other words: if one salvific narrative is fully true, then the differences in the other would be examples of deceptive corruption of that truth. So, if we test them by assuming their truth, which of the narratives better matches the pattern we would expect a corruption to have? (Should be the same answer as previous section)

font.b: What do those who deceive want? What is Satan's ultimate goal?

div.font: In both Islam and Christianity, Satan is the archetype of deception. His ultimate goal is to separate us from God: from rightly knowing Him and having faith in His mercy, from fulfilling our God-given purpose, and from accepting reality and living the truth that would earn God's pleasure. If what is real decides what is true, then his strategy ultimately reduces to corrupting our perception of reality, making us feel confident in what is fundamentally, partially, or even subtly false.

At a tactical level, this looks like lying about essential truths (about God, ourselves, and the world), repackaging falsehood as more coherent, comforting,, intuitive, or empowering than the truth, introducing precise distortions that simulate depth and complexity, magnifying extremes (exaggeration, reductionism, or otherwise imbalanced emphasis), blurring the line between ignorance/mystery and contradiction, and exploiting our vulnerabilities - ignorance, ego, despair, arrogance, tribalism, love of ease, desire for superiority, emotional volatility, misplaced identity, and worldly attachment - all so that we want the false narrative to be true.

div.b: What does deception look like? What is the epistemological difference between deception and correction?

div.font: If closeness to reality is closeness to truth (and thus to God), then the best deception is rarely the crude, obvious lie. Rather, it would be an almost-true narrative that feels coherent (using the truth to justify the falsehood), spiritually rich (masking contradiction as complexity), or emotionally satisfying (confusing comfort with truth) - diverging from the truth just enough, and slowly inching closer towards falsehood to avoid detection.

Epistemologically, this will always reduce to core contradictions being marketed as mysteries, paradoxes, or some other form of valid ignorance - manufacturing a false sense of harmony, and justifying coherence by appealing to ignorance when a clean correspondence with reality exists. As a result: if basic understanding of reality is required to identify the True religion, and if we assume that either Islam or Christianity is that True religion, then we can test their relative truth by comparing their differences to our basic understanding of reality - ascertaining which looks more like a corrupted version of the other (resulting in the other being its correction).

font.b: Justice is the settlement of sin's debt
Justice is the recompense/credit for both sin and righteousness

div.span: - Perfect justice is when the debt of every sin is paid - either by the sinner or a qualified substitute - and no human act or merit can undo it (on its own).
- God's law (including faith in God) doesn't erase guilt or restore communion: it exposes testifies against our sin - effectively condemning us.

- Federal headship: the actions of one individual can change the spiritual status of others (as with original/ancestral sin applying from Adam to us, and with Christ's atonement satisfying the debt for all humanity).

span.style: background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(237, 237, 237)); font-size: 8px;

b.style: background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(237, 237, 237)); font-size: 8px;

span.style: font-size: 8px; background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(237, 237, 237));

div.span: - Islam then changes this to justice being proportional accountability: all actions (both good and bad) have salvific weight, with each person judged only by their God-given capacity and carrying only their own burden.
- Neither human sin nor human righteousness occur "on their own": they both occur by God's will, and their spiritual impact also occurs by God's will.
- God's law (including faith in God) exposes both our good and bad: all our culpable actions will be justly recompensed.
- The law's emphasis on settlement shifts to accountability.
- Divine justice is embedded in the law - making federal headship unjust.

div.span: - Increasing accountability (justifying it using God's mercy)
- Increasing divine justice within the law

font.b: Justice is the recompense/credit for both sin and righteousness

div.b: Justice is the settlement of sin's debt

div.span: - Perfect justice is when every person is only responsible for what they do within their capacity, both with good and bad deeds.
- Every person receives proportional recompense (reward or punishment) based on the merit of their actions (for both good and bad deeds).
- Good deeds are multiplied out of God's mercy while sins are recorded as they are, and sincere repentance merits God's forgiveness by His leave.
- Christianity then changes this to the weight of sin being beyond human capacity to satisfy.
- The spiritual impact of righteousness is diminished in God's law, while the spiritual impact of sin is kept.
- Innocents can now bear others' burdens: with Adam's descendants being born in a fallen state, and with Christ satisfying the burden for all humanity

font.b: God expects sincerity with a finite set of obligations, only within one's capacity

div.span: - Out of God’s perfect justice, He expects perfection: every sin incurs a real debt that must be paid.
- As a result, the occurrence of any culpable sin severs us from perfect, holy communion with God - until later divine intervention restores it (with Jesus).
- Moreover,

span.style: background-color: transparent; font-size: 8px; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(237, 237, 237));

div.span: human righteousness (by itself) can't outweigh or cancel the cost of human sin (ie. recreating the state of grace that only God bestows).
- Islam then changes God's expectations to be the fulfilment of obligations with sincerity - with anything more being considered as "excellence".

- Sin still has a debt that can only be resolved by God's grace - which now manifests directly in the law itself: repentance and righteousness are both given salvific weight, capable of offsetting that of sin

Effective Changes
- God's fundamental expectation shifts from perfection to sincerity.
- Righteousness and repentance gain opposing power against sin.
- To embed God's mercy in His expectations, framing its as more original...
- ... without sacrificing justice, in holding us fully accountable to our sins

font.b: Mercy is embedded in the law

div.b: Mercy is not embedded in the law

div.span: - If God were to instantly hold us accountable to our deeds, we would all be punished (ie. natural negative consequence).
- God's mercy manifests in delaying that punishment (during life) - providing each of us the opportunity for righteousness, repentance, and forgiveness.
- Christianity then changes this by creating a division between God's law and God's grace, where the law condemns while His grace saves.

- We are still delayed from sin's eternal punishment, given the opportunity to turn to God for forgiveness in this life, and primarily saved by God's grace - but the law is no longer where His mercy and forgiveness manifest.
- An effective division between law and grace is added.

div.span: - Decreasing the reach of God's mercy (from the law)
